item.research_question: How does the morphology of CeO2 supports influence hydrogen spillover to enable the synthesis of sub-nanometer high-entropy alloy (HEA) clusters, and what are the resulting catalytic properties and structural reversibility under oxidative/reductive conditions?
item.material_system: CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters supported on CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs), CeO2 nanocubes (CeO2-NCs), and CeO2 nanoparticles (CeO2-NPs)
item.processing_route: Hydrothermal synthesis of CeO2 supports (NRs at 90°C for 24h, NCs at 180°C); impregnation of metal precursors (Co:Ni:Cu:Zn:Pd = 1:1:1:1:1) onto CeO2; reduction under H2 flow at 600°C without calcination
item.test_conditions: NO reduction by H2 (50–200°C); H/D exchange (300°C D2, then -50°C to 200°C H2); in situ XAFS under 8000 ppm NO/He and 20,000 ppm H2/He at 400°C
key_findings: CeO2-NRs with exposed (110) facets produced the most intense HD peak in H/D exchange, exceeding CeO2-NPs and CeO2-NCs by factors of 2.6 and 4.4, respectively.
CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs formed sub-nanometer clusters with an estimated diameter of 0.79 nm (average of 13 atoms) and a coordination number of 5.6.
The CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs catalyst achieved 100% NO conversion at 100°C, significantly lower than NPs (150°C) and NCs (200°C).
In situ XANES showed the Pd0 fraction in CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs remained at 0.78 after 30 min NO exposure, compared to 0.37 for monometallic Pd/CeO2-NRs.
FT-EXAFS revealed that under NO, short Pd–M bonds (2.1 Å) disappeared and long Pd–Pd bonds appeared, indicating sacrificial oxidation of non-noble metals.
DFT calculations showed NO adsorption energy on the HEA cluster was higher than on monometallic slabs, while H adsorption energy remained comparable.
The HEA13(Co2Ni2Cu3Zn3Pd3) cluster model reproduced a unique flat XANES post-edge shape, confirming the sub-nanometer solid-solution structure.
item.mechanism: Hydrogen spillover on reducible (110) facets of CeO2-NRs facilitates simultaneous proton-electron transfer, reducing metal cations with different potentials at low temperatures to form sub-nanometer HEA clusters. Under oxidative conditions, non-noble metals undergo sacrificial oxidation to form oxide shells around Pd cores (Pd@MOx), suppressing Pd oxidation and enabling structural reversibility upon reduction.
item.limitations: The text notes that synthesis of sub-nanometer HEA clusters remains challenging and that CeO2-NCs and CeO2-NPs resulted in phase-segregated or larger nanoparticles rather than uniform sub-nanometer clusters.
item.future_work: Further extension, including the detailed optimization of the components as well as their ratio, is under investigation.
quotes: The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts.
The fraction of Ce3+ in the material (Ce3+/(Ce3+ + Ce4+)) was found to increase in the order of CeO2-NCs < CeO2-NPs < CeO2-NRs.
The CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs exhibited the highest activity at lower temperatures, giving an NO conversion of 100% at 100 °C.

item.processing_route: pre-reduced by heating to 600 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min under a 20 mL/min flow of H2 and holding at that temperature for 2 h followed by cooling to room temperature
item.test_conditions: 50 mL/min flow of a NO/H2/He mixture containing 8000 ppm NO and 20,000 ppm H2; 50 mg quantity of catalyst in a quartz cell with an internal diameter of 4 mm
key_findings: Catalytic activities were evaluated using a fixed-bed reactor system.
Reaction products were analyzed with an online gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014 with a SHINWA SHINCARBON-ST column and a thermal conductivity detector).

Supporting Information includes HR-TEM, XRD, Tauc plot, H2-TPR, Cs-corrected SEM, HAADF-STEM, XANES spectra, FT-EXAFS spectra, XANES simulation, catalytic activity, DFT calculation, curve-fitting results at Pd K-edge for CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2, and lists of employed configuration patterns for adsorption energy calculations.
quotes: In each trial, a 50 mg quantity of as-deposited catalyst was transferred into a quartz cell with an internal diameter of 4 mm held between two portions of quartz wool.
Each specimen was pre-reduced by heating to 600 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min under a 20 mL/min flow of H2 and holding at that temperature for 2 h followed by cooling to room temperature.
Catalytic activity tests were then conducted under a 50 mL/min flow of a NO/H2/He mixture containing 8000 ppm NO and 20,000 ppm H2.
